entities.name: Miguel de Cervantes
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Miguel de Cervantes Saavedra (1547–1616) was a Spanish novelist, poet, and playwright whose 'Don Quixote' (Part I, 1605; Part II, 1615) is widely considered the first modern novel and the most influential work of fiction in the Spanish language. It has been translated into more languages than any book except the Bible.

Cervantes led a life as adventurous as his fiction. He fought at the Battle of Lepanto (1571), where he lost the use of his left hand, earning the nickname 'el manco de Lepanto.' He was captured by Barbary pirates and spent five years as a slave in Algiers before being ransomed.

Returning to Spain impoverished, he worked as a tax collector and was imprisoned at least twice. He began 'Don Quixote' reportedly while in jail. The novel's genius lay in its layered irony: a delusional knight-errant tilting at windmills became a profound meditation on reality, fiction, idealism, and the human condition.

Cervantes died on April 22, 1616—one day before Shakespeare. The Cervantes Prize (Premio Cervantes) is the most prestigious award in Spanish-language literature. As Dostoyevsky wrote: 'Don Quixote is the most profound and most lasting work of all literature.'

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Miguel de Cervantes' 'Don Quixote' is widely considered the first modern novel and has been translated into more languages than any book except the Bible, significantly influencing Western literature. Its impact on the development of the novel as a literary form cannot be overstated.
